short: A file with no pawns on it, or none of yours — the only thing that makes a rook useful.
body: A rook does nothing in the opening, which is why the principles tell you to castle, connect them and leave them alone. In the middlegame their entire value comes from files: a rook on an open file exerts pressure down the whole board, the same rook one square across is a spectator.

A half-open file — one where you have no pawn and your opponent does — is often better than a fully open one, because their pawn on it is a target that cannot run away. That is the mechanism behind the minority attack and most queenside play in the Sicilian.
Whoever puts a rook on a contested file first usually keeps it. If you see a file about to open, get there first, and think about doubling before your opponent contests it.

diagram.caption: White's rook takes the half-open e-file, pointing straight at e6.
